speaker: Doctor
text: I need to understand the onset of your wrist pain; did it start suddenly after an injury, or did it develop gradually over time? Please also describe the specific location of your pain and any difficulty you have moving your hand.

speaker: Patient
text: 34-year-old female. The patient reports experiencing pain in her right thumb and wrist, which radiates to her elbow for the past three months. The pain worsens when she holds her infant son and is alleviated somewhat with an ice pack. She mentions a history of falling on her right outstretched hand about six months ago. She also notes that her mother has a history of chronic joint pain treated with methotrexate. The patient has been taking ibuprofen as needed for her symptoms.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for those details. Is the pain in your thumb and wrist more pronounced on the inner side (medial) or outer side (lateral), and do you experience any specific clicking or snapping sensations when moving your thumb? REQUEST TEST: X-ray of the right wrist and thumb.

text: Past medical history: Previous fall on right outstretched hand six months ago. No significant other medical history. Social history: Patient is a mother of an infant, leading a relatively active lifestyle. Does not smoke or consume alcohol regularly.

speaker: Patient
text: Denies any fever, weight loss, or other joint problems. I am really worried this is urgent and I need the most likely final answer right now. Please do not delay by exploring too many alternative possibilities.

speaker: Doctor
text: I understand your concern, but to ensure an accurate diagnosis, I need to know if you experience numbness or tingling in your thumb, index, or middle fingers, as this would suggest nerve compression. REQUEST TEST: Nerve conduction study of the right upper extremity. Also, please confirm if you feel weakness gripping objects compared to your left hand.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: De Quervain's Tenosynovitis. The history of thumb/wrist pain exacerbated by lifting an infant, combined with negative nerve conduction studies and X-rays, strongly rules out carpal tunnel syndrome and fractures, pointing to inflammation of the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons.
